claims: US AI data-centre construction materially increases electricity demand over the next 12 months and beyond.
New data-centre load strains generation, transmission and interconnection capacity in key US regions.
Utilities and independent power producers can charge for, or invest profitably against, rising power demand.
Nuclear restarts and existing nuclear fleets gain value as sources of firm, carbon-free power for data centres.
Grid buildout increases demand for transformers, switchgear, automation, construction machinery and transmission.
Electrification and grid expansion increase copper demand for wiring, motors, transformers and transmission lines.
Power constraints, permitting and interconnection delays become a bottleneck for new AI data centres.
beneficiaries: Independent power producers with nuclear and gas capacity near data-centre clusters
Regulated utilities able to grow rate base through grid and generation investment
Copper miners and suppliers of electrical and construction equipment
Utility-scale solar and storage providers adding new generation capacity
losers: Data-centre operators facing higher power prices, delays or interconnection queues
Utilities without spare generation or transmission capacity in data-centre regions
Power-intensive users competing with data centres for scarce electricity
Projects dependent on slow permitting or scarce grid equipment

candidates.case: Vistra is listed in the universe for power, data-center, nuclear and grid themes, making its generation fleet the closest direct expression of firm power sold to meet rising load [E63]. This rests on general knowledge that Vistra operates merchant nuclear, gas and other generation rather than only regulated distribution.
risks: Merchant power prices may fall if new supply is built faster than demand, gas prices move against it, or nuclear outages and regulatory issues hit the fleet.

candidates.case: NextEra is listed for utilities, renewables, power and grid themes, so regulated utility investment plus contracted renewables directly benefit from more load and grid spend [E40]. This rests on general knowledge that it combines a large Florida utility with a major renewables and transmission developer.
risks: Regulators may limit allowed returns, interest rates may raise financing costs, and renewables or transmission projects may face permitting delays.

candidates.case: Duke Energy is listed for utilities, power, grid and defensive themes, giving regulated exposure to load growth, transmission and distribution upgrades in the US Southeast and Midwest [E18]. Its business is electricity delivery and generation, not a side division.
risks: Rate-case outcomes, storm costs, higher interest rates and slower data-centre siting in its territories could limit earnings growth.

candidates.case: Freeport-McMoRan is listed for copper, mining and electrification, and copper is a core input for transmission, transformers, motors and data-centre wiring [E20]. This rests on general knowledge that Freeport is one of the largest copper producers.
risks: Copper prices are cyclical and can fall on weaker global growth, new mine supply, substitution, or operational and political problems at mines.

candidates.case: Caterpillar is listed for machinery, infrastructure, construction and mining, selling equipment used to build power plants, transmission, mines and data-centre sites [E12]. It also rests on general knowledge that Caterpillar sells power-generation equipment including large gensets.
risks: Construction and mining cycles may slow, dealers may cut inventories, and data-centre backup power is only part of a broad industrial business.

candidates.case: Honeywell is listed for industrial, automation, aerospace and sensors, supplying controls, sensing and building and industrial automation that help manage power use and grid-connected facilities [E26]. This is a secondary supplier exposure, not a dedicated grid-equipment pure play.
risks: Honeywell is diversified, so grid and data-centre demand may be too small to move results, and industrial or aerospace weakness could offset it.

candidates.case: First Solar is listed for solar and renewables and, on general knowledge, supplies utility-scale solar modules that can add generation where data-centre load is growing [E21]. It expresses the new-supply side of the power shortage rather than regulated grid ownership.
risks: Solar policy, tariffs, interest rates, module pricing and project delays could hurt demand or margins despite rising power needs.

candidates.case: BIL is the SPDR Bloomberg 1-3 Month T-Bill ETF in the universe, used here for the requested 10% cash buffer rather than for the power thesis [E10]. That cash-like role rests on general knowledge of short-term Treasury bills; the quant evidence only covers its trading history.
risks: It will not participate if power and grid stocks rise, and its return will mainly track short-term Treasury rates, which can fall.

rationale_md:
## Thesis

AI data centres will keep adding large, concentrated electricity loads in the US, straining generation, transmission and interconnection capacity for years. If that holds, the winners are not only the data-centre owners but the companies that sell them firm power, build the grid, supply copper and equipment, and add new generation — while power availability becomes a constraint on AI growth itself.

## Why these holdings express it

The universe contains genuine pure plays on power and utilities, so the basket starts there. **VST** is the most direct name, listed for power, data-center, nuclear and grid themes [E63]; **NEE** combines utilities, renewables, power and grid [E40]; and **DUK** adds regulated utilities, power and grid exposure with a more defensive profile [E18]. Together they cover merchant firm power, contracted renewables and regulated rate-base growth without concentrating on one utility model.

Suppliers and chokepoints come next. **FCX** is the copper expression, listed for copper, mining and electrification [E20] — copper goes into transmission, transformers and wiring. **CAT**, listed for machinery, infrastructure, construction and mining [E12], sells the equipment to build sites, mines and generation. **HON**, listed for industrial automation and sensors [E26], is a more diversified supplier of controls and automation. The universe holds no dedicated listed pure play on transformers or switchgear, so that part of the thesis is expressed through these suppliers and the utilities' own capital spending, on general knowledge.

**FSLR**, listed for solar and renewables [E21], is an enabler on the new-supply side: more load creates more need for fast-to-build generation. **BIL** is defensive and implements the requested 10% cash buffer [E10]; its role as a 1–3 month T-Bill fund comes from its name and general knowledge, not from the price evidence. No leveraged or inverse products are used, in line with your constraint.

## Main risks

- Power demand from AI could grow more slowly than expected, or efficiency gains could reduce electricity per unit of compute.
- Utilities may not earn attractive returns if regulators resist rate increases or financing costs stay high.
- New generation, storage or transmission could arrive faster than expected, easing scarcity and merchant power prices.
- Copper and construction names are cyclical and can fall with the wider economy even if the long-term grid story is intact.
- Individual risks include nuclear outages at VST, rate-case outcomes at DUK and NEE, and policy or tariff changes for FSLR.

## What would change my mind

Evidence that US data-centre power demand is being cancelled or sharply delayed, that interconnection and grid investment are no longer bottlenecks, that utilities are unable to recover grid spending in rates, or that copper demand from electrification is weakening would undermine the take. Conversely, faster load growth alone would not fix poor regulatory returns — both demand and allowed returns need to hold.

*This is research to support your decision, not investment advice, and it does not promise returns.*
